activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
story:
Isla spread her notes across the library table and stared at the empty space where her conclusion should have been. Her science fair project was supposed to answer whether chewing mint gum helps people concentrate, and so far she had one story: her uncle, at Sunday dinner, holding up a copper bracelet. "Two weeks wearing this, and my back pain is gone," he had announced, tapping the table like a judge. "Proof right here." Isla had asked what else might have changed that month, and he had looked at her as if she had insulted the bracelet personally. She still wondered about that at odd moments, like now.

Elyssa dropped into the chair across from her, dumped a bag of sunflower seeds on the table, and pointed at Isla's laptop screen. "You should write about honey. I had a sore throat last week, my mom gave me honey tea, and the next morning it was basically gone. Honey works."

"Hmm," said Isla. She drafted a question on her notepad: What else might explain a sore throat going away overnight? She thought of her uncle's wrist.

"What," said Elyssa, who wanted credit for the idea and also, ideally, to be quoted in the project as a source. "It worked. That's my evidence."

"It's your story," Isla said. "One person, one time. Maybe your throat was going to get better anyway. Maybe you slept twelve hours. Maybe you drank so much tea the honey never got a chance to do anything."

Liana slid into the third chair, late and unwinding her earbuds. "My brother calls that an anecdote," she offered, stealing a sunflower seed. "A story about one person's experience. He says it can't show that one thing caused another, because other explanations haven't been ruled out." She said it fast, the way she recited song lyrics, and shrugged as if to apologize for having a brother who talked like that.

Isla wrote the word down. Anecdote. It fit her uncle exactly, and it fit Elyssa's honey, and it was somehow satisfying to have a word for the thing that had been bugging her since Sunday dinner. "So a claim needs tested evidence," she said slowly. "Not just a before and after from one person." She looked at her mint gum question with new interest. She could actually test it. She borrowed the sign-up sheet from Mr. Teo at the front desk, booked the library's back room for Saturday, and started listing things to keep the same for everybody: same puzzle, same time limit, same room.

"Fine," said Elyssa, cracking seeds, "but if the gum people do better, I want my honey story in the bibliography."

"That's not how bibliographies work," said Liana.

On Saturday, six classmates sat in the back room with identical puzzles, half of them chewing and half of them not, while Isla paced between rows of chairs with a stopwatch. The results sat dormant in her notebook, just numbers, not meaning anything yet. She would need to average them, and check them, and then whatever she found, she would report it, even if the gum did nothing, which she privately suspected. Her uncle, she decided, was getting a copy either way.

Elyssa chewed her piece of gum with visible determination, solved her puzzle, and raised her hand without being asked. "For the record," she said, "I also slept twelve hours last night, and my throat is still fine."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
story:
Andrew slapped two boneless chicken breasts onto the big wooden cutting board and grabbed the knife like a chef on a cooking show. Tonight was his night to cook, the first real one, and he had promised the family chicken with a big crunchy salad. He could already picture his little sister taking a second helping, which would be history in the making.

His phone buzzed on the counter. It was Cohen, who had taken foods class last semester. Making chicken? Get a pic. Andrew sent a photo of the pink breasts sizzling in the pan, proud of the even browning, and got back a thumbs up and one sentence that stopped him: Wash your board before the salad, dude. Cross-contamination is real.

Cross-contamination. Andrew turned the word over while he rinsed the knife. He had been about to chop the lettuce on the same board where the raw chicken had sat, board still damp from the meat juices. If bacteria from the raw chicken hitched a ride on the lettuce, the lettuce would never get cooked, so nothing would kill anything. The chicken was fine because the pan would do its job, but the salad went straight from board to bowl to mouth. That was the pattern, and it was invisible, which made it feel almost like a magic trick in reverse.

He decided to test it. He wiped the wooden board with a paper towel and held it under the light. It looked clean, genuinely clean, no pink, no smears. So why did he feel like it was lying to him? He dragged a finger along the grain. A faint slickiness caught in the grooves, the kind you would never notice unless you were looking for it. Looks clean and is clean are not the same thing, he thought, and grabbed a second board, the plastic one, from the cabinet.

"Two boards?" his dad said, wandering in and stealing a cucumber slice. "Fancy."

"It's proportional to how much I don't want anybody getting sick," Andrew said, snapping the lettuce into the bowl. "One board for raw meat, one for everything else." He shot a photo of both boards side by side and sent it to Cohen with the caption system in place.

The reply came fast: My hero. Then, from Cadence, who must have been in their group chat all along: wait, is that why my mom has a red board and a green board? It was a small irony, Andrew thought, that the color coding had been sitting in Cadence's kitchen his whole life and none of them had ever asked what it meant.

The chicken came off the pan golden, the salad crunched, and his sister did take seconds. Andrew stacked the dirty dishes by the sink, both boards on top, and called out, "I'm doing this again next week."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies, and the standing water helps keep many weeds from growing.
story:
Abigail had Ms. Karimi's question stuck in her head like a song she couldn't finish: by Friday, explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia. That was why she was halfway up the ridge trail with her backpack full of index cards, and why Scarlet and Brodie had agreed to come along and listen.

"Okay, one more time," Abigail said, stopping where the trail bent beside a rocky stream. "In summer the land heats up faster than the ocean."

Brodie flopped onto a flat rock. "You've said that four times. What does it actually do?"

That was the problem. She could say the words, but she couldn't see it, and it felt like reciting rather than understanding. She exhaled slowly and watched her breath drift off in the warm air, then pulled off her sunglasses, which had gone cool in the shade of her pack, and breathed onto one lens. It fogged instantly.

"Look," she said, holding them out. "Warm air from me hits the cold glass, and the water in my breath turns to droplets. So if warm, wet ocean air moves over hot land and then hits mountains, it rises, cools, and the water comes down as rain. Months of it. That's the monsoon."

Scarient took the sunglasses and tried it herself, breathing on the other lens until it clouded over. "Okay, that part I get. But who cares? Why does rice need all that rain?"

Abigail flipped through her index cards and stopped at the photo she'd printed, a green field that looked like a shallow lake with bright grass growing out of it. "I thought this was a mistake at first. Why would anyone flood their crop on purpose? Wouldn't it drown?"

"Maybe they just have too much water and no choice?" Brodie offered.

That didn't sound right. Abigail stared at the picture, thinking about her grandmother's vegetable garden and how much time she spent pulling weeds. Then the idea arrived all at once. "Wait. Rice grows fine in standing water, but weeds don't. The water smothers them." She pointed at the flooded rows. "Those fields are called paddies. The standing water keeps many weeds from growing."

"So the flood is doing the weeding," Scarlet said. "That's ironic. I'd have guessed the water was the enemy."

"Instead it's the helper," Abigail said. "And the monsoon fills the paddies, year after year. No monsoon, no water, no rice." She imagined what a failed monsoon would mean for a whole region of farmers, and the edge of that thought felt like despair, so she shook it off and got out her pencil.

Brodie leaned over her notebook. "Write the sunglasses part in. You fog the lens in front of the class."

"Ms. Karimi said no props," Abigail said, then grinned. "I'll just breathe on my own glasses and hand them to her."

She wrote fog on lens = rain on mountains, closed the notebook, and shouldered her pack. "Race you to the top," she said. "Whoever gets there last has to be the Indian Ocean."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
story:
Nathan had babysat exactly nobody before tonight, and now he was standing in Mr. Pereira's living room holding a seven-month-old who had been crying for twenty straight minutes. The baby, whose name was Sam, had a warm bottle, a dry diaper, and a clean blanket, and still the crying went on and on, like a fire alarm nobody could switch off. Nathan paced the carpet, bounced gently on his knees, and hummed every song he could remember from fourth grade. Nothing worked.

He texted Joanne, who had three younger cousins and therefore, in Nathan's opinion, knew everything. She replied fast: "Is he swaddled? Sometimes they just cry. What does your poster say?" Poster, Nathan thought. What poster? Then he remembered the one taped inside the pantry door, the one he'd glanced at while hunting for the formula. He carried Sam, still wailing, over to the pantry and read it under the dim bulb.

Shaken baby syndrome, the poster said in red letters. Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury. An infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head. Nathan read it twice, and a cold feeling crept up his arms. He had never once thought about what a baby's neck had to do. Sam's head was big compared with the rest of him, and when Nathan shifted him, the head wobbled like it was attached by a rubber band. So that was the hidden rule, the thing you couldn't see: the crying wasn't the danger, the frustration was, if you let it turn into shaking. The poster didn't explain more than that, but it didn't need to. Nathan looked at the crib in the corner and felt an idea take shape.

"Okay, buddy," he said out loud. "Here's my plan." He laid Sam on his back in the crib, made sure the blanket sat low around his legs, and stepped away to the couch. The crying kept going, muffled now, and Nathan sat with his hands pressed flat on his knees and breathed the way the track coach had taught them before a race. It felt almost inevitable that he would fail at this, that first-time babysitters always did. He reminded himself that Mr. Pereira had said Sam sometimes cried before naps, like a tiny storm that had to blow itself out.

He watched the clock. After four minutes, the crying dropped to a hiccupping whimper. After seven, the room was quiet. Nathan tiptoed over and peered into the crib. Sam's eyes were shut, his mouth a small round O, his head tipped safely against the firm mattress. Nathan grinned so wide his face hurt.

When Mr. Pereira came home at ten, he found Nathan washing a bottle in the kitchen sink. "How did it go?" he asked. Nathan dried his hands and pointed at the pantry. "Your poster saved us both," he said. "The storm passed at eight fifty-two."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
On the first humid morning of drama camp, Brooklyn froze in the middle of the black-box theatre while her partner, Brynley, mimed reeling in an invisible fishing rod. Brooklyn had no idea what she was supposed to say to a person holding nothing.

"Anything counts," Brynley said afterward, flopping onto the mats. "An offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, like a place, a name or a problem." She wiggled her fingers. "The rod was an offer. You just left me fishing alone."

Brooklyn thought about that all through lunch. Yesterday she had done the same thing to Destiny, standing there like a fence post while Destiny pretended to hand her a crying baby. Two partners in a row, and both times the scene had died. There had to be a pattern, and if there was a pattern, there was a rule she could test. On the walk back from the cafeteria, the air sticking to her arms, she decided her experiment: whatever her next partner offered, she would say yes and add something new.

Mr. Schneider split them into pairs and called Brooklyn up with Destiny again. "Show us a scene," he said, and stepped back against the mirrored wall, arms folded.

Destiny narrowed her eyes, then cupped her hands around her mouth like a megaphone. "Attention, passengers, we are now arriving at the moon base."

Brooklyn's mind went white for half a second. Then she spotted the offer, the place, hanging right there in the air. "Yes, and I'll grab our suitcases," she said, hauling two invisible bags off the invisible shuttle. "Grandma said she'd meet us at the airlock."

Destiny's whole face changed. "Grandma is the base commander," she announced, marching forward. "She said if you lost your luggage one more time, you'd have to conquer the laundry room alone."

"The laundry room is haunted," Brooklyn whispered, clutching her suitcase tighter. "Last summer she heard singing in the vents."

The audience on the mats dissolved into laughter. Even Mr. Schneider's shoulders shook once before he raised his hand to stop them. "Nice work accepting the offers," he said, and moved on to the next pair.

Afterward Destiny found Brooklyn by the water fountain. "Yesterday I thought you hated me," she admitted, pressing the button twice so the stream would run taller for Brooklyn's turn. "You just stared."

"I wasn't staring at you," Brooklyn said, bending to drink. "I didn't know the rules yet. I thought if I couldn't see the fishing rod, there was nothing there." She straightened up, grinning. "Turns out the nothing is the whole scene."

"Tomorrow you be the Grandma," Destiny said, already walking backward toward the mats, arms out like a shuttle. "I'll pick you up at the airlock."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Many proportional systems set a minimum vote share for winning seats; in Germany a party usually needs at least 5 percent of the national party vote, with limited exceptions.
story:
The courthouse rotunda smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Nicholas clutched his folder of mock election results like it was evidence in a trial. His class had voted last week on which project the county should fund, and Mr. Rao had brought them downtown for Youth Civics Day, where tables of sticky ballots lay spread out under a banner that read EVERY VOTE COUNTS. Nicholas's Parks Party had gotten exactly three percent of the vote. He was sure that meant something.

"Three percent of a hundred seats is three seats," he told Tea, pointing at the tally sheet. "I did the math twice on the bus."

Tea frowned at the numbers. "But look at the Greenway Party. They got eleven percent and only six seats. Something's not matching."

They spread the ballots on the bench. Lexi leaned over the pile, sorting votes into anonymous stacks so nobody could tell whose was whose. "Maybe it converts the percentages different than you think," she said. "Like, maybe there's a rule nobody told us about."

Nicholas tested it. He counted the parties that had won seats and the parties that had gotten nothing. The big parties all had over ten percent. The small ones, including his, sat at three, four, and two percent, all shut out. Every single seatless party was under five. He checked the handout Mr. Rao had left on the table, a single sheet comparing voting systems, and found one sentence buried near the bottom: in Germany, a party usually needs at least five percent of the national party vote to win seats, with limited exceptions.

"Five percent," he said quietly. "That's the line. That's why the numbers don't match."

"So your three percent gets you nothing," Tea said, not unkindly.

Nicholas felt a flush of empathy for the kid from the History Club whose party had gotten four percent, because now they were both on the same side of an invisible wall. Then he did the arithmetic again, and something worse turned up. Without the small parties taking seats, the Riverfront Party, the one that wanted to pave over the creek trail, had enough votes for a majority. His three percent hadn't just failed to help. By staying under the line, all the small parties together had handed the big one everything.

He raised his hand anyway when Mr. Rao called for final arguments. "I think the five percent rule protects against too many tiny parties," Nicholas said, hearing how reasonable it sounded, "but in our vote it also meant three parties' worth of voters got converted into zero."

Mr. Rao nodded and asked the class to cast one last vote, by show of hands, on whether to keep the threshold for next year's mock election. Nicholas voted against it, along with Tea and Lexi and the History Club kid.

The threshold survived, forty-two to thirty-eight, because the Riverfront voters had raised both hands.

"Every vote counts," Lexi read off the banner, and snorted. "Ours just counted for them."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
Christopher was trying to prove his grandfather wrong, which felt risky, so he waited until his grandfather went to the kitchen for more coffee before sliding into the desk chair.

The argument had started over dinner. A TV ad had come on claiming the city was about to tear up the old cargo docks and sell the land to a private company, and Grandpa had slapped the table and said, "See? That's what happens when nobody watches these people." Christopher's mom said the ad sounded exaggerated, and Grandpa said she was too trusting, and nobody had proof of anything. Christopher wanted proof. He typed the exact words from the ad into the search bar, half expecting to find nothing but other people yelling about it online.

Instead, a result came up near the top: PolitiFact, a fact-checking website founded in 2007. He clicked it. On the page was the ad's claim, word for word, with a little meter graphic beside it. The meter went from True on one end to Pants on Fire on the other. He leaned closer. The claim itself was rated in the middle, mostly false, with details underneath about what the city council had actually voted on.

"You're smiling," his mom said from the doorway, drying a plate. "What did you find?"

"A site that checks whether things are true. It rates claims on a scale called the Truth-O-Meter," Christopher said. "The ad only got a Mostly False. The worst rating is Pants on Fire."

Grandpa came back with his mug and stood behind him, reading over his shoulder. "So they're liars," he said.

"No, look," Christopher said, scrolling. "They're not liars, they're... stretchers. The council did talk about the docks. The ad just left out that the vote was about a study, not a sale." He pointed at the line. Grandpa read it twice, then grunted.

"Well," Grandpa said, "I still don't trust them."

"That's an opinion," Christopher said. "The ad is a claim. A claim you can check." He realized how it sounded and felt his ears go warm. "Sorry. That came out like Mr. Anderson."

His mom laughed. "It's fine. It's better than arguing." She set her hand on Grandpa's shoulder for a second, the way she did when she wanted him to know nobody was against him. Grandpa took his coffee to the window and watched the street while Christopher kept reading.

After a while Grandpa came back and tapped the screen. "So who checks the checkers? How do you know this site's not just picking sides?"

Christopher hadn't thought of that. He read the page again, slower this time, looking at where the quotes and documents were linked at the bottom. "They show their work," he said at last. "It's all transparent. Every source is right there."

Grandpa pulled the other chair over and sat down. "Show me the Pants on Fire one," he said. "That sounds like fun."

Christopher typed a new search and handed him the mouse.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: A toothpick pushed into the centre of a muffin that comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs shows the muffin is baked through.
story:
"Preheat the oven first," Paisley read aloud, "or the muffins sit in a cold box and sulk." She turned the dial to the number in Malak's grandmother's recipe and heard the oven click and hum.

Malak dumped flour into a bowl while Paisley cracked the eggs, and only one shell fragment escaped into the batter. "You can contribute that shell if you want," Malak said, fishing it out with a fingertip. "Extra calcium." Paisley threatened him with the wooden spoon, and by the time they stopped laughing, the batter was folded and the tray was filled with twelve lopsided dollops. The upstairs tenant, a quiet man named Mr. Okafor, leaned over the banister and asked what smelled so good, and Malak shouted, "Nothing yet! Come back in twenty-five minutes!" The timer was already ticking, because Paisley's mother was picking her up in exactly half an hour, and Paisley had promised to bring home six muffins for her sister's birthday breakfast. There was no room for a second batch if this one failed.

The timer buzzed, and Paisley pulled the tray out, but the tops looked pale, almost ghostly, and the middles wobbled when she tilted the pan. "They're not done," she groaned. "But the recipe said twenty-five minutes, and we have five left." Malak peered at the muffins like they might confess. "Maybe the outsides lie," Paisley said slowly. "Maybe we need to check the inside without cutting them open, because a cut muffin can't go back in the oven with any dignity." She grabbed a toothpick, pushed it into the centre of the biggest muffin, and pulled it out. The tip came out streaked with wet batter. "Not done," she announced, like a judge. She slid the tray back in and set the timer for five more minutes.

When it buzzed again, she poked the same muffin once more. This time the toothpick came out clean, with only a few dry crumbs clinging to it, and Malak cheered so loudly that Mr. Okafor thumped on his floor. "That's the test," Paisley said, jabbing a toothpick toward him through the ceiling. "Clean toothpick means baked through." She boxed six muffins just as her mother's car pulled up, and Malak kept six for his own slightly impoverished cookie jar, which contained, until now, exactly three stale crackers. "Next time," he called from the doorway, "I contribute the chocolate chips."

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: Reading a draft aloud often makes repeated rhythms and clumsy phrases easier to notice than reading it silently.
story:
Tyler sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with three paragraphs about the world's ugliest cat, and he hated every word he had written. His teacher, Mr. Huang, had written one comment in red pen at the bottom: "Cut the weak adjectives. Vary your sentence length. This reads like a drum beat." Tyler had read the note six times and still did not know what to do with it.

"You look like a man carrying a heavy couch," said his grandfather, setting down two glasses of lemonade. "Read me the thing. Out loud."

"Out loud?"

"Grandchildren read to grandparents. It's practically a law." Mr. Huang settled into the chair across from him, waiting.

Tyler read. Halfway through the first paragraph, his own tongue tripped him. "The cat was very big and very ugly and very grumpy and it lived in a very messy alley." He stumbled on the second "very" and had to start the sentence over, and that was when something clicked. He had read this draft four times last night and it had seemed fine. His mouth was finding problems his eyes had sailed right past. "Wait," he said. "Read it again," said his grandfather.

He read it again, and this time he heard the drum beat. Every sentence had the same shape, the same length, like a hammer hitting the same spot. "I keep saying 'very,'" Tyler said. "And everything's short. Short, short, short." He grabbed the pen and crossed out "very big" and wrote "the size of a backpack." He crossed out "very messy" and just wrote "the alley behind the bakery, crusted with flour." Then he joined two sentences into one long, rolling sentence, and let the next one stand alone, abrupt as a door slamming.

"It sounds like a person now," his grandfather said, "instead of a machine counting words."

Tyler read the whole revision aloud, and the paragraphs moved. Long, then short. Specific instead of padded. When his phone buzzed, it was Rayyan from the writing club, the one Aurelie had started because she wanted members who took the mystery genre seriously and kept complaining that everyone else wrote about dragons. "Did you fix your draft?" Rayyan texted. "Aurelie says if it's still all choppy she's making you read last."

Tyler typed back: "Read it out loud to yourself. Trust me. Your ears will catch what your eyes won't." Then he looked up at his grandfather, who raised his lemonade glass like a toast, and Tyler read the ending one more time, just to hear it land.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: The sense of smell naturally declines in old age, a change called presbyosmia.
story:
On the third morning of Grandpa's visit, the toast turned black again, and again he sat at the picnic table in Brielle's backyard, reading his newspaper, while smoke curled out of the kitchen window behind him. Brielle intervened before the whole slice went up in flames, waving a dish towel at the toaster until the smoke thinned. "Grandpa, didn't you smell it burning? The whole kitchen stinks." He looked up, surprised, and sniffed the air the way people sniff when they already know there's nothing to find. "Not a thing," he said.

That night Brielle lay in her sleeping bag on the floor of the screened porch, where Grandpa was camped out for the week, and turned the problem over in her mind. He had eaten the charred toast without a single grimace, and he hadn't complained once about the dilapidated compost bin, whose smell reached clear to the porch every afternoon, a smell strong enough that her friend Bodie refused to come through the gate during what he called the siege of the stinky bin. Brielle had a guess forming, and guesses, her mother always said, were only useful if you tested them.

The next afternoon she set up her experiment on the porch steps. She lined up five jars with holes punched in the lids: cinnamon, coffee grounds, an orange peel, vinegar, and a slice of onion. Simran came over to watch, notebook in hand, ready to record results like a proper assistant. "One at a time," Brielle said. "Say what you smell, or say nothing if you smell nothing." Grandpa closed his eyes, willing and cheerful, and held each jar under his nose. Coffee, he got. Cinnamon, he got, faintly. The orange, the vinegar, and even the onion, nothing at all, though Simran's eyes were watering from two feet away.

When they called her mother out to try, she named all five without hesitating and then got every single one right even through the closed lids, which Simran said was showing off. Brielle looked at her grandfather, who was laughing at the face Simran made. She thought about the years of Sunday dinners at his house, how he never once commented on the food, and how she used to believe he simply didn't care. That judgment felt different now, sitting unfinished inside her. "Grandpa," she said, "do you think maybe it's just what happens when people get older?" He nodded, calm as anything. "My doctor told me the word for it once. Presbyosmia." Simran wrote it down letter by letter and underlined it twice.

After supper, Brielle dragged the smoky toaster out to the backyard table, unplugged, and set a jar of cinnamon beside Grandpa's chair where the evening breeze would carry it to him. She would watch the toast herself from now on. Simran flipped to a fresh notebook page and wrote tomorrow's experiment at the top: which smells survive best. Grandpa picked up the cinnamon jar, breathed in, and smiled. "That one," he said, "I'd know anywhere."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Shabbat, the Jewish day of rest, begins at sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday.
story:
Owen had hypothesized that surviving one Saturday without screens at Grandpa's house would be easy, since he'd survived a whole week of camp once with only a postcard. But that was before Friday evening, when Grandpa slid Owen's phone into a wooden drawer in the hallway and said, "Shabbat now, buddy. It begins at sunset on Friday." Owen stood with his hand still shaped around air, staring at the drawer as if his phone might reappear if he was diligent about it.

"But the sunset isn't even finished," Owen said, pointing at the window, where orange light was still smeared across the sky like jam. "I can literally still see the sun's leftovers." Grandpa laughed so hard he had to sit on the arm of the couch. "Leftovers. That's a good one. It begins at sunset, and it ends after nightfall tomorrow, Saturday. Nightfall, not lunchtime, so don't try the sunset trick twice." Owen flopped backward onto the cushions. He had planned to test exactly that trick, and now his whole experiment was ruined before the first trial.

Saturday morning, Owen found Jordan and Malak already at the kitchen table, because their parents had dumped them at Grandpa's for the day too. Malak was building a tower out of stale pretzels, and Jordan was teaching the toaster to accept bread in a gentler manner. "What do you even do all day?" Owen asked. Jordan shrugged. "Argue. Eat. Grandpa tutors me in chess and loses on purpose, I think." Malak whispered, "He doesn't lose on purpose. Jordan is just weirdly good."

So Owen became a scientist of the day of rest. He timed Grandpa's chess moves and discovered that Grandpa lost only when Malak was watching, which meant the losing was not about chess at all, it was about making Malak feel the morning was worth attending. He tested the pretzel tower's balance against three different foundations. He raced Jordan to see who could name more constellations out the kitchen window, using only a book with a cracked spine called The Night Sky, and he lost twice and won once, by naming the Big Dipper in under a second, which Jordan claimed should be disqualified for being too obvious.

When the sky finally turned properly dark, after nightfall the way Grandpa had promised it would, the drawer slid open with a small wooden groan. Owen's phone screen lit up with eleven notifications, and he looked at them, then at Malak's tilting pretzel tower, then at Grandpa holding out the black queen from the unfinished game. "We were in the middle of something," Grandpa said. Owen put the phone face down on the counter and picked up his knight. "Check in two moves," he said. "Hypothesize all you want, buddy. It's check in one."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: Have I Been Pwned, a website launched by security researcher Troy Hunt in December 2013, lets people check whether their email address appeared in a known data breach.
story:
Anthony had used the same password since second grade: lizardking99. It worked for his library account, his game account, and now Mr. Ortiz wanted everyone to make an account for the class science portal. The trouble was that the portal rejected it. "Too common," the screen said, in polite red letters.

"It's not common," Anthony muttered. "Nobody else likes lizards that much."

Marguerite leaned over from the next computer. "It's not about lizards. It's that hackers have giant lists of passwords people already used. If yours is on a list, it's like hiding a key under the doormat."

Anthony didn't believe her, exactly. How could a list know his password? But during lunch he asked his grandfather to text him the email address he used for everything, and in the computer lab he typed it into a site Fateh had told him about, a site called Have I Been Pwned. On the screen it said his grandfather's address had shown up in a known data breach, one from years back.

"Whoa," Anthony said. "It says Grandpa's email got leaked in a breach. The site's been around since December 2013. Some security researcher named Troy Hunt made it."

"So change his password," Fateh said, spinning a pencil. "And don't reuse the old one anywhere."

That was the part Anthony finally understood, like watching a decomposer break down a log in science class: invisible things doing real work. If someone had Grandpa's old password, they could try it on every account Grandpa owned. Using it twice didn't just break a rule, it violated the whole idea of a lock.

He built a new password out of four random words and a number, long enough that it looked eccentric, like a stranger's name. He typed it twice, wrote a hint on a card for Grandpa, and folded the card into his pocket.

At home that evening, he slid the card across the kitchen table. "Grandpa, we need to talk about your doormat."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
story:
Anthony had measured everything he could measure. Two inches taller since September, shoe size up twice, and a chin hair he refused to call anything until it was distinct enough to count as real. But the thing happening inside his throat was invisible, and that was starting to intimidate him. His voice had gone rogue, cracking on simple words like "here" and "fine," and he wanted a reason he could actually test.

He wrote a note to his friend Anders before class: Meet me in the health room at lunch. Bring your answers. I have data. Anders sat behind him in fifth-grade choir, and Anthony still remembered the day Anders opened his mouth for a high note and a sound came out like a sliding whistle, half squeak, half groan. The whole risers had shaken with laughter. Now, two years later, Anthony was the one making that sound, and nobody was laughing, especially not him.

At lunch, Anders found him at the back table in Mr. Bui's health classroom. Anthony had a page of tally marks. "Every crack this week," he said. "Eleven. Guess what else is new. I sang low this morning and it felt easy. Actually easy."

Mr. Bui, watering the plant by the window, glanced over. "Your larynx is growing," he said, and went back to the plant.

Anthony looked at Anders. "The larynx. That's the voice box, right?" Anders nodded. Anthony grabbed the anatomy poster from the shelf and found it, then traced downward with his finger. "There are vocal folds inside it. If the box is growing, the folds are getting longer and thicker. Longer strings on a guitar sound lower. That's my whole theory. My voice is dropping because the parts are changing size, and it cracks while the growing is still going on."

"So how do you test it?" said Anders.

"Already did. The cracks cluster in the afternoon, when my throat's tired. Growing parts need rest. Tomorrow I talk less in the morning and sing low on purpose."

Anders grinned. "Puberty is basically the last frontier, and you're mapping it."

Anthony wrote one more line on his page, underlined it twice, and stuck the poster back on the shelf. "Fifth period," he said. "Watch me hit the low note."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
story:
Sebastian slumped into a seat near the back of the 42 bus, his backpack heavy with a science quiz he had probably failed. Above the window, a new ad showed a basketball player he recognized holding a bottle of TurboFizz. "Champions drink TurboFizz," the ad said, and beneath that, in smaller print, "Nine out of ten riders agree." He had seen the same ad on four different buses this week, plus two billboards, and somewhere in his head a voice had started saying it like it was a fact, the way you know water is wet. Yousif dropped into the seat beside him. "My mom says we should boycott that stuff," Yousif said. "Too much sugar. But everybody at school drinks it. Even Barrett, and Barrett hates soda." Sebastian dug out his crumpled homework sheet, the one he was supposed to read before the quiz, and smoothed it on his knee. One paragraph near the bottom caught his eye: In 1977, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true. He read it twice. The bus hissed to a stop and the conductor, who checked passes at the front when the machine broke, called out, "Move back, please, all the way back."

"Yousif," Sebastian said slowly, "how many times have you actually seen somebody prove TurboFizz does anything? Not the ad. Proof." Yousif shrugged. "It's everywhere. It has to be good." Sebastian tapped the homework sheet. "That's the thing. Repetition. I've seen that ad maybe ten times this week, and it feels true just because I've seen it ten times. The study says people rate statements as more likely true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they're true. Whether or not." He decided to test it. "Nine out of ten riders agree. There are, what, twenty people on this bus? If the ad's real, most of them should agree."

He stood up, wobbling as the bus turned, and started asking. "Excuse me, do you drink TurboFizz?" A man with headphones shook his head. A woman laughed and said it tasted like cough syrup. Two kids near the front said yes, and one of them only said yes because the basketball player on the ad was his favorite. Out of eighteen riders, four agreed. Sebastian sat back down, heart pounding a little, and did the math on the back of his hand. "It's not nine out of ten. It's four out of eighteen. The ad just repeats itself until it sounds like everybody." The bus stopped again and Mr. Andersen, their neighbor, who rode this route every evening, looked up from his newspaper. "Quiz today, Sebastian? You look like a boy who found something out." "I did," Sebastian said. He held up the sheet. "Turns out my brain believes things it's just heard a lot. I thought that was a TurboFizz fact in my head, but it was only a TurboFizz habit."

The bus rattled on past the lit shop windows, and the basketball player grinned down at them from three ads in a row, the same grin, the same bottle. Yousif leaned over and pulled a TurboFizz can out of his own bag, then looked at it for a long moment like it had said something embarrassing. He held it up toward Sebastian. "Conventional wisdom says I bought it because it tastes good." He dropped it into the trash can by the door, where it clanked against the metal and rolled to a stop. "Four out of eighteen," he said.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Lines of latitude are also called parallels because they never meet, and lines of longitude are called meridians.
story:
Lily knelt on the floor of the tent with the old atlas Ms. Korhonen had lent her, tracing her finger along the thin lines that crossed every page. The rain drummed on the nylon above her, and Steve and Leandre sat beside her, waiting for it to stop.

"Ms. Korhonen said whoever finds the coordinates of the town nearest our campsite gets to cook first," Steve said. "Which means you get the extra marshmallows."

Lily ran her finger along a horizontal line toward the edge of the page. "These sideways ones are the ones we need," she said. "They're called parallels, because they never meet." She pointed at the vertical ones next. "Those are meridians."

"How can they never meet?" Leandre asked. "They go all the way around."

Lily remembered her grandmother's globe from last summer, how she had spun it slowly in the dim living room while everyone else talked in the kitchen. She had traced two lines with her thumb then, watching them ride alongside each other across the whole curved world, never touching, and she had decided it was probably some kind of printing mistake. Now she wondered whether she should have asked about it instead of shrugging and putting the globe back on its shelf.

"Look at the map," she said. "They stay the same distance apart, all the way across. Parallels." She tested it with the atlas, sliding her pencil flat between two of the lines. The pencil stayed snug from one edge of the page to the other. On the vertical lines, though, the pencil caught almost right away, because those lines bent together toward the top of the map. So the sideways lines were the true parallels, and the meridians were something else. The gap between meridians implied that the map was squeezing the world flat somehow, and that the squeezing wasn't the same everywhere.

"So which one's which number?" Leandre asked.

"Parallel first, then meridian," Lily said, checking the numbers printed along the edges. She found the line that ran just under their campsite, then the meridian that crossed it, and wrote both numbers on her hand with a ballpoint pen. The spacing between the printed lines was proportional to the distance on the trail, she noticed, so a small distance on the map meant a small walk in the rain. Their town sat close to the crossing point.

"Close enough to be the nearest one," she said. "Unless there's a smaller dot I'm missing."

"Every dot matters when marshmallows are at stake," Steve said, and leaned over her shoulder as she turned the page.

"Forty-four and counting," Lily murmured, running her pencil along the parallel one more time, all the way to the edge of the paper, where it still hadn't touched the line above it.

"Got it," Steve said. "Now hand me that piston of a flashlight before we lose the light."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: Scratch, a block-based programming language, was developed at the MIT Media Lab and first released in 2007.
story:
Oliver leaned so close to the basement monitor that his nose almost touched the screen. Christophe's cat sprite was supposed to dart around a maze and gain a point every time it touched a coin, but the score kept jumping from one to nine in a single blink. "That's impossible," Oliver said. "Nobody collects nine coins that fast."

"Maybe it's haunted," Christophe said, grinning from the beanbag chair. Oliver didn't believe in haunted games, but he did believe in bugs, and this one was hiding somewhere. He decided to hunt it the way Ms. Dela Cruz had taught them: change one thing, watch what happens, change another. First he slid the "change score by one" block out of the loop and clicked the green flag. The score stayed at zero. So the block worked fine on its own. Then he put it back and slowed the loop way down. The score ticked up one, two, three, then leapt straight to nine. The bug wasn't random. It followed a pattern, and patterns meant rules.

"The if-then," Oliver said suddenly. He opened the coin's code and found the problem: the if-then block checking "touching cat" was sitting inside the coin's own loop, so it fired nine times before the coin had a chance to hide. He dragged the hide block up so it ran first, clicked the flag, and watched the score climb honestly, one point at a time. Christophe shot out of the beanbag like a cork. "You fixed it! You actually fixed it!"

Upstairs, Christophe's grandfather called down that it was time for snacks, and when he came to the bottom of the stairs he squinted at the tangle of colored blocks on the screen. "You children are doing real programming with... puzzle pieces?" He sounded the way people sound when they see a dog walking on its hind legs. "Coding is all typing, isn't it? Endless lines."

Oliver straightened up proudly. "It's called Scratch. It came out of the MIT Media Lab in 2007." The grandfather leaned in, tapped the screen gently, and said that in his day you needed punch cards and a whole week to make a computer do anything. He asked whether the games were durable enough to survive an eleven-year-old's little brother, and Christophe promised that Oliver was about to integrate a train conductor sprite who would chase the cat, which would absolutely guarantee the little brother's attention for hours.

The conductor was Christophe's idea, a stern little figure in a blue cap who was supposed to shout "Ticket, please!" whenever he got close to the cat. Oliver built the if-then, wrapped it in a loop, and set the sound to play. On the first test the conductor shouted ticket twenty times a second, a wall of noise that sent the grandfather back up the stairs laughing and made both boys cover their ears.

"Dude," Christophe wheezed, "fix that before my mom hears it." Oliver grabbed the wait block and slid it into the loop. "One ticket at a time," he said, and hit the green flag.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each half of the Hindu lunar month, is a fasting day dedicated to Vishnu on which many Hindus avoid grains and beans.
story:
Sara had noticed something odd about her grandfather: twice in the last month he had pushed his plate of rice away and eaten only fruit and milk, and when she asked, he just smiled and said, "Today is a special day for Vishnu." Twice a month felt too regular to be random, so she did what any serious investigator would do. She taped a calendar to the fridge, grabbed a marker, and circled every day Grandpa refused rice.

"That's not a lot of evidence," said Rami, who was sprawled on the kitchen floor dismantling an orange to see if it could be rebuilt into a smaller orange. "Two circles. My little brother draws two circles on the wall and it doesn't mean anything."

"It means something if they're spaced right," Sara said. She counted the days between the circles. Eleven, then eleven again. Then she flipped back further and checked the days against the moon chart in her astronomy book, because her grandfather's "special day" always seemed to follow the moon. The eleventh day after each new moon and the eleventh day after each full moon, there they were, both circled. She ran to the living room. "Grandpa, is it called Ekadashi?"

His eyebrows went up. "Ekadashi," he agreed, tapping his newspaper. "The eleventh day. A fasting day for Vishnu. No grains, no beans."

"That's the word!" Sara shouted, so loudly that Edwin, who had come over to borrow markers, dropped three of them.

The problem arrived that evening, and it wore a party hat. Rami's birthday sleepover was planned for Saturday, with a giant pizza and a movie marathon, and Saturday, Sara realized with a chill, was an Ekadashi. Pizza was basically bread, which was grain. She had until Saturday to figure something out, because the one thing she refused to do was skip the party.

She tested her idea on Friday. If she was going to keep the day the way her family did, she needed practice, so she ate no rice, no bread, and definitely no beans, even though the cafeteria's chili was ninety percent beans. "You're avoiding the chili," Edwin said, watching her steer her tray past it like it was a live volcano. "Nobody avoids the chili voluntarily."

"I'm training," Sara said, and she munched her apple with dignity.

At the party, while everyone attacked the pizza, Sara sat with a bowl of fruit and a glass of milk, and Rami, being a good friend, had quietly bought her a small watermelon. "Happy birthday to me," he announced, "and happy Ekadashi to you." Grandpa, dropping her off the next morning, looked at the empty watermelon rind and gave her a slow nod of respect.

"One more thing," he said at the door. "Eleven days from now, it comes again. Mark your calendar."

"I already did," Sara said, holding up her phone with the reminder set.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
The lobby filled up at 7:58, and Layla counted the names scrolling up the side of the chat: Aleksandar, Leonidas, two strangers with numbers in their handles, and her. Leonidas typed "ready" with no punctuation. Aleksandar typed "Ready." with a period, and somehow it looked like he was annoyed with everyone before the match had even started.

"Your brother is mad," Layla said into her headset.

"He's not mad," Aleksandar said. "He typed ready."

"He typed ready with a period. It's like when Mom texts 'Fine.' You know something bad is coming."

Aleksandar laughed, but Leonidas cut in. "It's literally the same word."

Layla wasn't so sure. She'd read something once, in the waiting room of the dentist's office, about researchers at Binghamton University. A small study from 2016 had found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one. She'd thought it was funny at the time. Now it seemed like evidence.

"Okay, test," she said. "Leonidas, ask me if I liked the new map. Then watch."

Leonidas asked. Layla typed "yeah" and sent it. Then she typed "Yeah." and sent that too.

"See?" she said. "First one's fine. Second one, I sound like I'm doing you a favor."

"That's insane," said Leonidas, but he was quiet for a second. "The second one does kind of sound like that."

"Because it's a rule," Layla said. "Somebody studied it. Small study, 2016, Binghamton. Periods make you sound less sincere in texts."

Aleksandar gasped in mock horror. "You believed a magazine in a dentist's office? You're so gullible."

"I'm not gullible, I'm observant. Watch this." She typed to one of the strangers, "nice shot." A moment later, she typed "Nice shot." at the other one. The first stranger replied with three thumbs up and a friend request. The second one replied, "you being sarcastic?"

"Point proven," Leonidas said.

The match started and everyone stopped typing, which was the lobby's other unspoken rule. Layla revised her plan for the group chat she ran with the robotics club: no more announcements ending in periods, especially not "See you all Thursday." That one had gotten her two worried replies last week and she'd finally worked out why.

After the match, Aleksandar sent her a private message instead of typing in the lobby. "Okay," it said, no period. Then, in the public chat, for everyone to see: "gg."

Layla smiled and typed back, "gg."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate.
story:
Taylor had one hour before the archive closed, one worksheet due Monday, and one very smug friend named Noel leaning over her shoulder. "You have to use a primary source," he said, tapping the page of the settler's diary Ms. Popescu had pulled from a gray box. "Like that."

"I know what a primary source is," Taylor said. "I was listening. Mostly."

The diary belonged to a farmer named Mr. Alden who had trudged west in 1849, and Taylor's job was to explain why he went. Easy, she thought. He wrote that the fields back home were worn out and that his cousin had sent a letter about rich land near the river. Done. She started copying the quote, then paused. Alden claimed he set out on March 3, the day the whole town saw a comet hang over the church steeple. Taylor frowned at the sentence. A comet. Over a whole town. That felt like the kind of thing other people would have written down too.

"Newspapers," Noel said, pointing at a shelf. His reflex for showing off was faster than Taylor's reflex for saying thank you. They carried a bound volume of the town paper to the table and turned the pages for March 1849, Taylor checking each date with one finger. March 1, nothing. March 2, an advertisement for cough syrup. March 4, a report of a barn fire. Then, on March 12, there it was: a paragraph about a bright comet seen across three counties, "remarked upon by nearly every citizen." Taylor sat back so fast her chair squeaked.

"So the diary says March 3," she said slowly, "and the paper says March 12. One of them is wrong. But which?" She looked at the diary again. Alden had terrible handwriting, the kind where a one and a two could be twins, and his ink had blotched right through the second digit. She turned to Noel. "Maybe he wrote twelve and it just looks like three. Or maybe the paper got it wrong." They dug further, and Noel found a stack of letters in another box, including one from Alden's cousin. "He says here, 'We watched the comet from the porch on the twelfth,'" Noel read, in his dramatic narrator voice. Two sources against one, and Taylor felt something click into place, like a puzzle piece that had been hiding under the table the whole time. Historians, she realized, did exactly this. They checked a diary against letters, newspapers, and government records to test whether its details were accurate, so they could distinguish a reliable account from a flawed one.

"You look way too happy about a comet," Noel said.

"I'm happy about being right." Taylor copied the March 12 date onto her worksheet, then added a line about how she knew. The worn fields and the cousin's letter still explained the move west, and those details matched the land records Ms. Popescu brought over in a folder. Taylor grinned at her two distinct sources, side by side, agreeing with each other.

At the front desk, Ms. Popescu stamped Taylor's worksheet with a rubber stamp shaped like a tiny archive. "Come back Thursday," she said. "We have a set of letters with a suspicious amount of tea stains."

"Tea stains?" Noel perked up.

"Distinguishable from coffee," said Ms. Popescu, "if you're careful."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
The standings sheet went up on the rink bulletin board every Monday, and Zack checked it first thing. His name sat in fourth place out of twenty skaters in the time trials, one spot behind Anthony and two behind Karissa. Fourth meant he'd made the travel team. It also meant he was "behind" the top three, and he wanted to know by how much.

"That list doesn't tell you anything," Karissa said, pulling on her gloves beside the bench. "It just says who's ahead of who."

"It tells me I'm fourth," Zack said.

"It doesn't tell you if you're a hundredth of a second behind me or a whole minute behind me."

Zack stared at the board. He had never thought about that. A hundredth of a second and a whole minute were both just "third is better than fourth." The ranking squashed them into the same thing. He decided to test it.

During warmups he asked Mr. Sadeghi, who ran the clock for the league, if the raw times were written down anywhere. Mr. Sadeghi flipped through a binder and found a printout. Zack ran his finger down the column. Karissa's best time was 34.12 seconds. Anthony's was 34.13. One hundredth of a second apart, and the sheet showed them as first and second, as if one of them had crushed the other. Then Zack found his own time: 34.15. Three hundredths behind Karissa. Almost nothing. Almost the same race.

"I thought you were way ahead of me," he told Karissa at the blue line.

"See? The board lies by not lying," she said. "First and second could be a hundredth apart or a whole minute apart. Same one and two."

Zack decided to stop reading the standings and start reading the times. That became his new ambition for the season: not to climb the list, but to shave real tenths off his own number. He kept the printout folded in his sock drawer, and he cherished it more than the medal from last year's tournament, because the medal only said he'd won and the paper said how close everything had been.

At Friday practice the coach split them into scrimmage lines and put Zack out against Anthony, the way he did when he wanted the fastest skaters matched. In the first minute Anthony cross-checked him lightly in the corner and gave him a look that could only be called venomous, though they'd been friends since second grade.

"Puck's still in play," Anthony said.

"Everything's still close," Zack said, and drove past him toward the net.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
story:
Nathan stood at the kitchen doorframe where the pencil marks climbed like a messy ladder, one for every birthday, and noticed that the last three marks were almost two inches apart while the ones from when he was nine had barely moved. He had shot up so fast this spring that his ankles showed below his jeans, and his shoes, which had fit in September, pinched by March.

That afternoon his dad had taken him to Dr. Patel's office about his knee, and she had put his leg in a machine that hummed. On the glowing screen, his bones looked like pale branches, and near each end there was a thin dark line. "Those are your growth plates," she had said. "Bones grow longer at the growth plates near their ends. Once the plates close after puberty, you stop getting taller." Nathan had stared at the thin lines and thought, so that is where the growing happens, hidden away inside, like a factory nobody can see.

Now, in the kitchen, he wondered whether his own plates were still open or already closing, and how a person could even tell. He fetched a pencil, stood with his heels against the wall, and made a careful mark at the top of his head. Then he devised a plan so simple it almost seemed silly: he would measure himself every Sunday morning, before breakfast, for the rest of the year. If the marks kept climbing, his plates were still open for business.

Lennon came over after dinner, and Nathan showed him the doorframe and the fresh mark. "You're doing a science experiment on yourself," Lennon said, grinning. "Sort of," Nathan admitted. "The growing happens at the ends of the bones, in these things called growth plates, and once they close after puberty, that's it, you're done." Lennon stood against the wall too, and Nathan marked him, then wrote the date beside it in small letters. Lennon was a full inch taller, which made him a useful candidate for comparison, a second experiment running in parallel.

Thalia, who lived next door, knocked on the back door holding a plate of cookies her mom had sent over. When Nathan explained his Sunday measurements, she frowned at the doorframe. "But how do you know you're not just standing taller some days? My grandma says I sit up straighter when I'm nervous." Nathan had not thought of that. Slouching could shrink a mark by half an inch, easy. So he added a rule: heels against the wall, chin level, measured at the same time each week. It felt good to control the variables, even ones as small as a morning slouch.

Weeks passed. The marks crept up, an eighth of an inch here, a quarter there, then two Sundays with no change at all, and Nathan hovered over the ladder of pencil lines like a detective over footprints. He caught himself checking his knees in the shower, looking for some sign, but the plates kept their secret. Still, the rising marks were proof enough. Somewhere near the ends of his bones, in those dark lines on the X-ray, something was still quietly at work.

On a Saturday in June he woke to find his ankles showing again below cuffs that had reached his shoes in May. He pressed his knuckles against the doorframe and traced the newest mark, the highest one yet, half an inch above Thalia's Sunday line. "It's still open," he told Lennon on the phone. "Sunday, same wall, bring your sister's measuring tape."

Lennon laughed. "You're going to do this until we're thirty."

"Until the marks stop moving," Nathan said, and he penciled the date beside the newest line.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'putting or placing under'.
story:
Leah pressed her palm against the mirror maze wall and counted her reflections. Somewhere behind the glass, a fan was supposed to be running, because the sign said moving air circulated through the exhibit to keep the mirrors from fogging. But the glass in front of her had gone cloudy at the bottom, and no breeze touched her wrist. She wanted a good idea for her science fair board, and a foggy mirror in a science centre seemed like a place to start.

Hadi found her with her ear against the glass. "You look like you're spying on the maze."

"I'm checking if the fan is running. I can't see it, so I have to guess from what I can see." She pointed at the fog. "My guess is the fan stopped, or something is blocking the vent."

"That's a hypothesis," Hadi said. "Mr. Goldberg made us write one on the board last week. A testable guess, he said, that an experiment can support or overturn." He pulled out his phone. "I looked the word up for my board. It comes from ancient Greek. It literally means 'putting or placing under.'"

Leah stepped back from the glass. "Putting under. Like placing your idea under the evidence and seeing if it holds it up." She liked that. Her guess was under the fog, waiting to be tested. "Okay, so if the fan is broken, the fog should be worst near the vent, and there should be no air moving anywhere. If the vent is just blocked, maybe some air still circulates on the far side."

They walked the perimeter of the maze, taking turns holding out strips of paper from Hadi's notebook. Near the exit, on the opposite wall, Leah's strip lifted and fluttered. She laid her hand flat against the glass there. It was clear, cold, dry. The fan was running. The vent was blocked. Her first guess was overturned, and she felt the small jolt of that, the ground shifting under an idea she had liked.

Alexie came out of the maze looking lethargic, dragging her feet and fanning herself with a pamphlet. "It's stuffy in there. I almost fell asleep between two mirrors." Leah showed her the fluttering paper, then the fogged glass near the blocked vent, where a plastic banner had slipped down over the grate. A staff member came by, lifted the banner away, and within a minute the fog began to shrink from the edges inward. Leah wrote in her notebook: hypothesis, from ancient Greek, putting or placing under. Under the evidence, the blocked-vent idea had held.

Mr. Goldberg was standing by the Tesla coil with his class, and Leah waved him over. "You were right about hypothesis," she said. "Mine got overturned first, and it felt like losing."

"Then it worked," he said, and tapped her notebook with one finger. "Write the overturned one down too. That's the half nobody ever puts on the board."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted.
story:
The food bank had invaded the library's meeting room overnight, and Grace was staring at six crates of donated bananas with a problem. "They're all spotty," said Colin, holding one up like evidence in a courtroom. "Nobody wants spotty bananas."

Grace turned one over in her hands. The peel was brown in patches, but when she pressed it, the fruit inside felt firm. She peeled a corner, and the banana underneath was pale and perfect. "The spots are just on the outside," she said. "It's like judging a book by its cover. This is a library, Colin. We of all people should know better."

"Big inference from one banana," Colin said, but he grinned and peeled one too. It was fine. They both peeled a second one to be sure, which was really just an excuse to eat bananas.

Ms. Toussaint hurried past with a clipboard. "Distribution opens at noon, everyone. That's ninety minutes, and we still have three crates of produce to sort." Grace noticed that Ms. Toussaint kept setting the spotted produce aside in a separate pile, the way you'd set aside a book with a torn cover for repair. Hmm, Grace thought. If the whole town judged fruit by its peel the way Ms. Toussaint just did, how much perfectly good food was getting tossed?

She wasn't guessing, either. There was a folded pamphlet on the sign-in table, and she smoothed it open. The U.S. Department of Agriculture, it said, estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted. She read it twice. "Colin. Between 30 and 40 percent. Of the entire food supply."

"That's like four out of every ten bananas never getting eaten," Colin said slowly.

"Thirty to forty out of every hundred," Grace corrected, "but yes. Four-ish out of ten." She held up a spotty banana. "And this is why. People see spots and think garbage."

At eleven forty, Grace made her move. She set up a table by the door with a sign that said FREE: UGLY BUT DELICIOUS FRUIT, and beneath it she copied the fact from the pamphlet, numbers and all. Then she did a vigorous demo, peeling a speckled banana in front of everyone like a magician revealing a card. The fruit inside was flawless. Audrey, sorting cans nearby, started applauding, and a few early visitors gathered around.

The twist came at noon, when the first woman in line picked up a spotted banana, examined it, and said, "Oh good. My kids only like them when they're spotty. The sweet ones are too plain." She took six.

"The sweet ones are the plain ones," Colin repeated, staring. "We had it backwards the whole time."

Grace pushed the last crate toward the table. "Then grab a peel. Ugly fruit, coming through."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
At dinner Blake pushed his noodles around his plate and waited for the right moment. Tomorrow he had to give a five-minute presentation on his family's heritage for Ms. Vu's class, and his plan was to convince his parents to let him skip it. He had his argument ready. "My heart was pounding today when Ms. Vu picked the order," he said. "Like pounding. And nothing dangerous was even happening."

His dad didn't look up from his plate. "You're not skipping a presentation."

"I didn't say skip. I said maybe switch to a poster." His dad waved a hand, the way he dismissed anything that sounded like complaining, and Blake felt his frustration rise. That was the stress of it, his mother called it, the pressure that built up before something big. His older cousin used the word anxiety for the same thing, the worry that showed up even when there was nothing to worry about.

Then Crosby, who was over for dinner again because his mom worked late, leaned forward with his whole upper body. "Wait. Why does your heart pound if nothing's dangerous? That makes no sense."

"It's actually a thing," Mika said from the counter, where she was helping cut fruit. "There's a fight-or-flight response. Your adrenal glands release adrenaline, and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing speed up." She said it like she was reciting from a poster in the nurse's office, which she probably was, since she'd spent a week there with her broken wrist.

Blake set down his fork. His body had noticed the presentation was coming and reacted like a bear had walked in. His heart and breathing were just doing what adrenaline told them to do. So maybe, he thought, the trick was not to fight the feeling but to work with it. He had read that slow breathing was a coping strategy, something people used to settle themselves down. He could test that right now, before he even asked about the poster again.

He breathed in slowly through his nose, counted to four, and let it out even slower. He did it three times while his dad told Crosby a story about a significant spelling bee disaster from fourth grade, which made everyone laugh, including Blake's mom, who had heard it nine times. His pulse felt steadier. His shoulders came down from where they'd been living, somewhere near his ears.

"So can I do the poster instead?" Blake asked, one more try.

"No," his dad said. "But you can practice it on us right now."

Blake stood up, wiped his hands on his jeans, and faced the dinner table. "My great-grandmother came here with one suitcase and a recipe for apricot cake," he began, and his heart thumped once, hard, like a drum checking if it was still needed.

"Slower," said Crosby, mouth full. "And start with the cake part."

Mika set a bowl of fruit on the table. "Boundaries, Crosby. He's presenting, not serving dessert."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: A chapati puffs up on the heat because water in the dough turns into steam.
story:
Dominic stared at the three stations in Ms. Navarro's cooking class like a general studying a battlefield. The rice had to boil for eighteen minutes, the curry needed a slow fifteen, and the chapatis would take barely a minute each. "The whole point," Ms. Navarro announced, "is that everything lands on the table hot at the same time. Team that manages it gets bragging rights until June." Dominic grinned. His team was him, Ziad, and Jonathan, and he intended to earn those rights.

"Start the rice first," Jonathan said immediately. "It takes longest." Dominic counted backward instead: rice at minute zero, curry five minutes later, then chapatis in the final stretch. He poured the rice into the pot himself, even though he secretly resented how easily Ziad had claimed the curry station, the one that smelled like cinnamon and toasted spices. The chapatis were the leftover job, plain dough and a hot pan, and Dominic was stuck with them.

Then Ziad ruined everything, or seemed to. He tipped too much water into the curry and stood there holding the jar, looking guilty. "That's the end," Jonathan groaned. But Dominic looked at the pale ball of chapati dough and thought about the water Ziad had spilled, and then about the water already hiding inside the dough itself. Every dough had some water mixed into it, didn't it? And water, when it got hot enough, turned into steam. Steam took up more room than water. He rolled a circle flat and laid it on the pan.

The flat disc sat there doing nothing. Dominic refused to stay neutral about it; he leaned in, watching. Then the edge went pale, the surface tightened, and the whole circle ballooned up off the pan like a small golden pillow. "Whoa!" Jonathan shouted across the room. "It blew up! Ziad, look!" Ziad abandoned his curry and came running. "It's puffing because of the steam," Dominic said, hardly believing his own words. "The water in the dough turns into steam." Ziad slapped the counter. "You're telling me there's steam inside bread?"

Dominic tested it. He pressed the next puffed chapati flat with a cloth, and warm damp air hissed out of it, fogging his fingers like a mirror in a steamy bathroom. Steam. It had been in there all along, hidden, waiting for heat. He could not see it before, but now he had proof. Ms. Navarro drifted past and said only, "Nice puff," which felt like a medal.

The clock hit minute eighteen. Dominic slid three ballooned chapatis onto the plate beside the rice while Ziad spooned the curry, and everything steamed together at once, perfect and simultaneous. Jonathan raised a spatula like a sword. "We are unstoppable," he declared. "Nobody can defeat us." Dominic laughed and pointed the spatula at him. "Wrong. We finally defeated the real antagonist of this class. Cold rice."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
The poster outside Mr. Brown's office door showed a calm blue lake, and David read it twice before knocking. His hands were still shaky from the math quiz. Not because he hadn't studied, but because the moment Mr. Reed said "begin," his mind went white, and he had to guess on half the problems. He wanted to fix that before the next one, and Mr. Brown's office was where kids went when something like that needed fixing.

Inside, the room smelled like lemon polish and old paper. Mr. Brown waved him to a squashy chair by the window, where late sun made a warm square on the carpet. Cody was already there, slouched with his arms crossed. He had been sent for throwing his binder across the gym after losing three straight scrimmages. "I'm not angry," Cody kept insisting, though his ears were red.

"I get stressed about quizzes," David admitted. "Like, a lot." Cody laughed once, without much humor in it, and Mr. Brown nodded slowly and asked what each of them did afterward, on a bad day. That was when Finlay stuck his head in the door, looking for David. He'd been hoping all week that David would finally come watch his brother, an artisan who carved wooden spoons at the market, and had promised to introduce them after school. Finlay leaned on the doorframe and joined in anyway.

"Easy," Cody said. "I slam stuff, then I stay up till midnight playing games so I don't have to think about it." He shrugged. Finlay shook his head. "My sister says coping means the ways you handle stress or difficult feelings. Slamming stuff and staying up all night is the bad kind." David turned that over. He thought about how he felt after a run, how the worry seemed to drain out of his legs, and how his mom always asked about his day and somehow things got smaller when he told her. "So the healthy kind is exercise," he said slowly, "and enough sleep, and talking to someone you trust." He looked at Cody. "You do the opposite of all three."

Cody glared at the carpet for a long moment. Then he said, so quietly David almost missed it, "My grandpa used to take me to the court at seven in the morning." He'd stopped going because he decided he was too slow to ever be good, and he had refused every invitation since. "Fine," he muttered. "Seven tomorrow. But if I miss every shot, nobody laughs."

They shook on it. On the way out, David paused at the door and turned back. "Same time next week? I'll tell you if the quiz thing worked." Mr. Brown smiled and tapped the blue lake poster. "Seven in the morning counts as exercise," Cody called down the hall. "Bring a ball."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Answering an insult with another insult tends to escalate a situation, while a short, calm statement like "That's not funny, stop" gives nothing new to fight about.
story:
Owen sat on his bedroom floor with his phone propped against a pillow, watching a screenshot circulate through the seventh-grade group chat. Somebody had taken an awkward picture of Ciara in gym class, mouth open, one shoe flying off mid-sprint, and by dinner time it had reached three different chats and at least one kid Owen didn't even know.
