Under the picture, someone had written "Cheetah Girl" with nine crying-laughing faces.

He had already tried to fix it once, that afternoon at school. When Marcus had crooned "Cheetah Girrrl" across the cafeteria, Owen fired back with the cleverest thing he could think of on the spot. "At least she can run, Marcus. You got winded carrying your lunch tray." For one glorious second the table laughed at Marcus. Then Marcus got louder, meaner, and invented three new names for Ciara before the bell rang. Owen had made it worse, and he knew it, and the knowing sat in his stomach like a rock.

He tried an experiment right there on his bedroom floor. He typed insults into a notes file, imagined Marcus's face after each one, and deleted them one by one, because every clever line he imagined ended with Marcus having something new to grab onto. It was like handing a person in a food fight extra ammunition and being surprised when they threw it. What Owen needed was something with nothing to fight about. Short. Calm. He typed it out: That's not funny. Stop.

Before he could lose his nerve, the doorbell rang. It was Ms. Hoang, the tenant from the downstairs apartment, holding a plate of lemon bars because, as she put it, "the recipe made too many, which is a lie, I made too many on purpose." She noticed his phone screen and his face. "Bad day or bad math homework?" she asked.

"Bad comeback," Owen said. "I tried to defend my friend and it turned into a whole thing." Ms. Hoang handed him a lemon bar and said only, "Try it a different way," which was exactly useless and exactly right. He went back upstairs, opened the group chat where the screenshot was still bouncing around, and posted his five words. Then he set the phone face-down and ate his dinner, because watching would have driven him crazy.

When he finally looked, the chat had gone quiet. Two kids had typed "fair enough." Marcus had sent a shrug emoji and changed the subject to Friday's game. And Ciara had sent Owen a single private message: "Thanks. Also, tell your downstairs neighbor I can smell those lemon bars from the bus stop." Owen grinned and typed back, "Come get one. She made too many on purpose."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, all lines going straight back into the distance meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, at the viewer's eye level.
story:
Muhammad stood at the window of the art room with his sketchbook propped against the sill, staring down at Elm Street where it ran from the school gate toward the traffic lights. Ms. Clarke had set the assignment on Monday: draw a street that looked real, one that seemed to go back into the distance instead of lying flat on the page. So far his street looked like a shoebox lid. The two edges of the road ran side by side, perfectly parallel, all the way to the edge of the paper, and the sidewalk lines did the same. It looked like a map, not a street.

"I'm entering mine in the front hall display," Francois said, sliding his own drawing across the table. "Louis-Felix says only two drawings get picked, and I want mine to be one of them." His street was better than Muhammad's, but something about it was strange too. The left edge of his road slanted toward the top right corner, the right edge slanted toward the top left, and the sidewalk lines converged somewhere near the middle of the sky. The buildings on either side leaned inward like they were tired.

Muhammad remembered the summer before, at his cousin's camp, when they had walked the main road at dusk. He had stood at one end and noticed that the road, which he knew was the same width all the way along, looked like a wedge narrowing to a point, and the telephone poles, all the same height, shrank toward that same spot. He hadn't thought about it since, but now he wondered whether that shrinking was a real phenomenon, something the world actually did to straight lines, or just a trick his eyes had played once.

He decided to test a hypothetical version on paper. He drew a flat line across the page and marked a single dot on it. "That dot is my eye," he said quietly. "The line is the horizon." Then he drew the road edges so that both of them, left and right, ran back to that one dot, and he sent the sidewalk cracks and the building rooflines and the shopfront edges to the same dot. Every line that went straight back into the distance ended at that single point, sitting on the horizon line exactly at eye level. He added windows, and those lines went there too.

The street popped. It looked like you could walk into it. He tapped the dot and told Francois, "This is called the vanishing point." Francois leaned over and frowned at his own drawing, at its three different meeting spots scattered around the sky.

"That's why mine looks like the buildings are falling," Francois said. He despised erasing, always had, because it smudged and tore his paper, but he picked up his eraser anyway and swept away the crooked lines. "Help me find my horizon?"

They worked until the bell, both streets narrowing toward their own single dots. Ms. Clarke stopped at the table on her way past and looked at the two drawings for a long moment, then at the dot Muhammad had labeled in small letters.

"Two drawings get picked for the display," she said, and pinned them both to the corkboard by the window, side by side, their vanishing points pointing down Elm Street toward the traffic lights.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass.
story:
The campfire crackled in the ring of stones, and Noemie watched a spark spiral up past the dark pines. It was her first night at Lake Birch Camp, and her counselor had promised s'mores before lights-out at nine. Nine was the deadline for everything here: fire out, teeth brushed, and, according to the schedule taped to the cabin door, nightly tick checks.

"Tick checks are for babies," said Daxton, from the log across the fire. "I'm not letting Rex pick through my hair like a monkey."

"Monkeys groom each other all the time," said Rex, who seemed to know a lot of facts nobody asked for. "It's a social thing."

"Great, then it's social. Still not happening."

Noemie turned her marshmallow over the coals. Before the bus left that morning, her mother had cornered her in the driveway with a laminated card from the health office, and Noemie had skimmed it just to escape. Somewhere in the fine print it had said that in parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass. At the time she'd thought, fine, whatever. Now she was thinking harder, because today's hike had gone straight through a meadow of grass taller than she was, lush and waving, the kind you crash through on purpose because it feels like a movie.

Here was the problem she turned over while the marshmallow browned: a tick was small, and the meadow had been big, and if one had hitched a ride it would be somewhere on her right now, hidden, doing whatever ticks did instead of introducing themselves. She couldn't see the cause. She could only test for it. She could check, or she could not check and find out in three weeks by feeling terrible. Even Daxton's math was good enough for that.

The fire was dying and the counselor called ten minutes to lights-out, so Noemie stood, brushed off her shorts, and said, "Rex, check the back of my neck. My mom's card says blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease in this part of the country, so we're supposed to check after hiking through tall grass. We hiked through tall grass today. Lots of it."

Rex came around the fire and peered at her neck like a doctor. "You're clear. Behind your ears?"

"Clean."

Daxton lasted about forty seconds. Then he sat down on the log next to them, faced away, and pulled his collar down without a word. "Just the neck," he said. "Just the neck, and nobody mentions it."

Rex leaned in, went quiet, and then said, "Hold still."

Behind the fire's last orange light, Noemie watched Rex frown and reach out very carefully with two fingers.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In American English, a comma or period that ends a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks; British usage often places it outside.
story:
Zachary slid his notebook across the library table so fast it nearly knocked over Casey's juice box. "Read line twelve," he said. "Tell me what's wrong with it."

Casey squinted. "She said, 'I'm not afraid of the antagonist." The period sat outside the quotation mark, small and wrong-looking, like a shoelace untied on the last hole. "You marked that exact thing wrong on my paper last week," Casey said. "Mr. Yip circled it in red."

"That's the problem," Zachary said. His story was due in forty minutes, last period, and his pen pal Eshan had marked up his draft before mailing it back from Manchester. Every single quotation ended with the period or comma outside the closing quotation mark. Every one. "Either Eshan can't punctuate at all, or something weirder is going on."

Amanda dropped into the third chair, chewing the end of a pencil. "Weirder how? Punctuation is punctuation." The library smelled like old glue and the lemon cleaner the janitor had used on the shelves, and somewhere behind the biography section a kid was giggling at a book about an eccentric inventor who lived inside a piano.

Zachary flipped to the appendix of his grammar book, the one nobody ever read, and found a footnote. He read it twice. "Okay. Listen. In American English, a comma or period that ends a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks. British usage often places it outside." He looked up. "Eshan's British. He wasn't fixing my mistakes. He was fixing them his way."

Amanda leaned over the table. "So his corrections look like errors to us, and ours look like errors to him?"

"Try it," Zachary said, and he allocated the last three pages of his notebook to an experiment. He wrote the same sentence twice, once with the period inside, once outside, and showed them to Casey. "Which one would you mark wrong?" Casey pointed at the outside one. Then Zachary wrote the sentence on a slip of paper and handed it to the librarian at the desk, asking casually which looked right to her. She tapped the inside one without hesitating.

"So it's not a rule rule," Amanda said slowly. "It's more like which side of the ocean you learned on."

Zachary grinned. His story still needed a climax, and now he had one, a real one. He wrote fast: the narrator's eccentric grandmother, the antagonist neighbor who stole her prize pumpkins, and at the peak of the story the two of them arguing over the garden fence. He made sure the final line ended with a period tucked neatly inside the quotation marks. Then, underneath, he added a note to Mr. Yip: "If the punctuation in my draft looked British, that was on purpose."

He was sprinting for the door when Casey called after him, "It wasn't on purpose!"

"It is now," Zachary said, and held the notebook above his head like a trophy.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Cutting an onion in half from top to root and laying each half flat side down gives a steady base, so the onion cannot roll while you slice it.
story:
"Okay, sauce master," Ryland announced, dropping three tomatoes and one enormous onion onto the counter. "Tonight my parents get real pasta sauce, not the jar stuff. You in?"

Mason was in. He'd been begging his mom to teach him to cook, but she always said later, so when Ryland invited him over to attempt it from scratch, he'd said yes before Ryland even finished the sentence. Chanelle was there too, phone propped against the sugar bowl, because she wanted to film the whole thing for her cooking channel. "My subscribers love disasters," she said cheerfully. "No offense."

Mr. Iyer, the neighbour who had lent them his good knife, had said exactly one thing at the door: "Fingers like a claw, knuckles forward." Then he'd gone back to his own garden. Mason curled his fingers and practised the claw against the cutting board while Ryland wrestled the wobbly table by the window. The whole onion sat waiting, round and smug.

It rolled. Mason set it on the board and reached for the knife, and the onion slid sideways, bumped the edge, and dropped straight off the table. It rolled under the chair. He retrieved it, set it down harder, and it rolled again, like it had a plan. "It's mocking you," Chanelle said from behind her phone. Mason stared at it, thinking. Round things roll, that was the problem, but the onion wasn't round all over. It had a top with papery skin and a root with little hairy roots at the bottom. If he cut it in half from top to root, each half would have a flat side, and a flat side wouldn't roll. He could lay each half flat side down and it would sit steady. He tried it, blade straight down through top to root, and the two halves sat there on the board like they'd been glued.

"Yes!" Chanelle zoomed in. "That's going in the video. Actually, forget disasters. I'm calling this one Pro Tips with Mason." She'd changed her mind about the whole angle, which was fine with Mason, since his knuckles were doing real work now, guiding the knife while his fingertips stayed tucked safe inside the claw. Slice by slice, the onion fell into neat half-moons, and his eyes streamed anyway. "If onions ever go extinct," he wheezed, "I will not be sad."

They cooked the onion until it went soft and golden, stirred in the tomatoes, and let the sauce bubble while Ryland made a pot of pasta. When his parents sat down and took the first bites, his dad looked up with an expression Mason hoped would be permanent. "You made this? All three of you?"

Mason grinned, chopsticks of steam still rising off his own plate. "Wait till you see episode two."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
Rosalie pushed her peas around her plate and waited until her father looked up from his noodles. "I need eleven dollars," she said. "By Saturday."

"Eleven dollars for what?"

"Strawberries. There's a girl at the farmers' market who sells them in little wooden baskets, and they're the best ones I've ever had. I want to get one for Troy's mom. She just had surgery, and Troy said strawberry shortcake is her favorite thing in the world."

Her father raised an eyebrow. "Eleven dollars for one basket?"

"Maybe two baskets. Last month they were five fifty each, but I only had three dollars then, so I couldn't get any. Now I have six."

At school the next day, Rosalie sat with Jeremiah at lunch and counted her money again, as if coins might have multiplied overnight. "Six dollars and forty cents," she said. "Shortcake needs a lot of strawberries. A lot."

Jeremiah frowned at her pile of quarters. "Wait. Your mom told my mom those baskets were five fifty in June. Why would the price go up?"

Rosalie stopped stacking the quarters. That was a good question. Things didn't usually just get more expensive because time passed. She tried to think of an objective reason, something based on facts instead of guesses, but all she had was a hunch that didn't feel solid. "Maybe I remembered wrong," she admitted. "Maybe it was the grocery store that was five fifty."

After school they walked to the market together. The strawberry stand was easy to find because the line in front of it stretched past the honey table and halfway to the kettle corn. Rosalie's stomach dropped. Long lines meant everyone wanted them, and if everyone wanted them, the price would be even higher. Her plan might evaporate before she even reached the counter.

But when she finally got there, the sign read "Two seventy-five a basket." Rosalie stared at it, then counted the baskets stacked behind the table, rows and rows of them, more than at any stand around it.

"Two seventy-five?" she asked the girl at the register. "I thought they were five fifty."

"They were," the girl said, wiping strawberry juice off her hands. "That was back in June, before the local ones came in. It's peak harvest now, so the farmers have the most they'll have all year, and everybody drops their prices."

Rosalie did the math so fast it felt like the numbers jumped at her. Two baskets for five fifty. She had enough for four, plus cream. She could make the shortcake, and there would be leftover strawberries for Troy's little brother, who Jeremiah said had been eating cereal for dinner all week while their mom recovered.

On Saturday, Rosalie carried the baskets to Troy's house in a paper bag that smelled like summer. Troy opened the door, saw the red tops through the paper, and changed his mind about something right there in the doorway. He had been planning to say she didn't have to do all that. Instead he said, "Come in. My mom wants to meet the person who did this."

In the kitchen, Troy's mom sat with her foot up on a chair, and Rosalie washed the berries at the sink while the oven ticked warm behind them. "Four baskets," Troy said, peeking into the bag. "How?"

"Timing," Rosalie said, and slid a perfect strawberry across the counter to Troy's little brother, who caught it in both hands.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, thee is the object form of thou, the way me is the object form of I, so "I love thee" means "I love you".
story:
John tapped his pencil against the desk and read the line again. "Hear my prayer, and hear my speech." That one was easy. But three lines later the speech said "thee," and two lines after that it said "thou," and John could not tell why the word kept changing. Mr. Sato had appointed each group a scene to paraphrase into modern English by Friday, and John's group had Romeo's speech from the balcony scene, which was mostly Romeo saying the same thing to Juliet in different ways.

Maliyah slid her paper across the table. "I got 'thou art fair' as 'you are pretty.' Then it says 'I love thee,' so I wrote 'I love thee.' That's not paraphrasing, but I don't know what else to do with it."

"Mr. Sato will count that wrong," Theron said. He was copying the speech onto translucent overhead film, which Mr. Sato still used even though the projector was older than any of them. "Half the words are thee and half are thou, and I can't see a pattern."

John looked down the page. "It is my lady, O it is my love." Thou there. "O that she knew she were." Then, a few lines later, "see how she leans her cheek upon her hand, O that I were a glove upon that hand, that I might touch that cheek." Thee, in "the brightness of her cheek would shame those stars, as daylight doth a lamp," no, wait, that one had no thou or thee at all. John started over, more carefully.

"I see it," he said. He grabbed a fresh sheet and wrote two columns. "Where the word is doing something, like 'thou art,' it's thou. Where something happens to the word, like 'I love thee,' it's thee." He tested it against every line in the speech. "The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars." No test case there. "As daylight doth a lamp." None. He skipped to the lines he had marked. "What if thou art fair, and 'I love thee.' Try it, Maliyah."

Maliyah read both columns. "So 'I love thee' means 'I love you.'"

John nodded. "Thee is the object form of thou, the way me is the object form of I. You wouldn't say 'I love he,' you'd say 'I love him.' Same thing here."

Theron looked up from the overhead film. "Run it through the whole network of lines and see if it breaks."

They went line by line, all three of them, Theron reading, John marking, Maliyah writing the modern English underneath. "See how she leans her cheek upon that hand" became "look at her resting her cheek on her hand." "'O that I might touch that cheek' stays almost the same. Every thou was a subject, every thee was an object, and not one line broke the pattern.

At the front of the room Mr. Sato called for volunteers. John raised his hand before he thought about it, and carried the overhead film to the projector, sliding it onto the glass while the class went quiet.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
Carson typed his message into the class discussion board and pressed enter before Ms. Mehta could finish her sentence about the voting project. "Great, so our proposal to cancel recess is basically approved," he wrote, grinning at his screen. Around the computer lab, nobody was grinning back.

Adriel turned around so fast his headphones nearly flew off. "We never voted on that. Ms. Mehta, Carson says recess is cancelled." Three other heads popped up over their monitors like prairie dogs. Linda raised her hand and said, in a voice way too calm, "Carson, that is a controversial thing to post on the official board." Her tone made it sound like he had threatened the school itself.

"It was a joke," Carson said. His ears felt hot. "Obviously a joke." But it was not obvious, and that was the problem. The board stripped everything down to flat gray words. No grin, no shrug, no eye roll. His joking voice had worn no camouflage at all, and every reader had walked right past it and believed him. Ms. Mehta just said, "Public posts get read literally, Carson. Fix it," and moved on, which somehow felt worse than a lecture.

He deleted the post and stared at the blinking cursor. Then he devised a test. He typed a new message: "The vending machine now accepts homework as payment :-)" and sent it to the private chat window he shared with Adriel and Linda, not the big board. Linda replied in seconds with a single "ha." Adriel sent back a row of laughing faces. Same kind of joke, different result. So what actually changed? Not the words. Something about the room itself, the audience, the mark at the end.

At home that night he dug around, and there it was, on an old university page. A computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, exactly so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Carson sat back. Somebody forty years ago had hit the very same wall he had just hit in fifth period, and had typed a tiny sideways smile to solve it.

The next morning he walked into the lab early, opened the class board, and posted a correction. "Yesterday's recess message was a joke. I forgot the :-). Invented 1982 for people exactly like me." Then he waited by the door, arms crossed, watching the room fill up. Adriel was the first to sit down and read it. He looked over at Carson and said, "You looked this up at home?" Carson tapped the side of his nose and said, "September 19, 1982. Look it up yourself."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The plain-folks technique presents a politician or company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as "one of us."
story:
Alexis slid her history textbook across the desk and pointed at a poster Arham had just finished taping to the wall. It showed Arham grinning over a tray of cafeteria mac and cheese, with the words VOTE ARHAM: JUST ONE OF US printed underneath in fat red letters. "That's due in ten minutes," she said, "and I don't know what it's selling."

"It's selling me," Arham said. "Mr. McKenzie said campaign posters, so I made a campaign poster. I'm running for student council."

Macey leaned over from the next row, chewing her pencil. "Okay, but what's your actual plan? Like, what will you do if you win?"

Arham blinked at her. "Plan?"

Alexis looked from the poster to Arham to the clock above the whiteboard. Down the wall hung the other posters, and she noticed something she hadn't before. One said EVERYBODY'S VOTING FOR TESSA, which couldn't literally be true since nobody had voted yet. Another said DON'T LET THE GREEDY CAFETERIA BOSS WIN, though Alexis was pretty sure there was no cafeteria boss, greedy or otherwise. A third showed a photo of the school's retired gym teacher holding a thumbs-up next to the words HE'D VOTE DANIEL. None of them said what anyone would actually do. They weren't posters about plans; they were posters about feelings. The mac and cheese photo fit the pattern, too, and she flipped through her textbook to the chapter they'd skimmed last week until she found the word she wanted. "Plain-folks," she said, tapping the page. "That's the one you're doing. It makes you look ordinary so people trust you like one of us."

"So it works?" Arham said hopefully.

"It works like mac and cheese works," Alexis said. "It gets attention. But Macey asked you a real question and you didn't have an answer." She tested the idea out loud, mostly to hear how it sounded. "Maybe a poster with a plan beats a poster with a fork."

Arham's shoulders dropped, and Alexis saw that his hands were still tight on the tape. He wanted this, badly, more than he'd let on. "I can't redo it," he said. "Ten minutes."

"You don't have to redo it. You need a plan, on paper, next to the photo. Macey, help him. You wanted vending machines with juice last month; make him say it."

Macey was already scribbling. "Juice, and a second bench by the field, and club photos on the hallway board. Say them out loud so I can get the words right."

"I could mediate," Alexis offered, holding up the tape, "between him and the wall. You write, I'll hang."

Mr. McKenzie drifted past with his coffee mug, a vessel so old the handle had been glued twice, and paused at the row of posters. "Two minutes," he said mildly. "Also, whoever wrote THE GREEDY CAFETERIA BOSS might want to know we have a lovely cafeteria manager." A ripple of laughter went down the rows, and the boy who'd made it went pink and started peeling his poster off the wall.

Macey handed Arham the finished sheet. Her handwriting was small and precise, and the last line read, in her neat letters, "I'll ask for juice, a bench, and a photo board, and I'll report back every month." It wasn't eloquent, and it wasn't supposed to be. Arham read it, nodded once, and said, "That's actually me. I mean, I'd actually do that."

"Then tape it up," Alexis said, and pressed the strip of tape into his hand just as the clock ticked to the deadline.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: The Jewish afterlife is often called olam ha-ba, meaning the world to come, though the phrase itself does not appear in the Hebrew Bible.
story:
The reunion was at Aunt Denise's house, and Jace had one job before the potato salad ran out: find out what happens after you die, according to at least two people who did not agree. He had a notebook. He had a pen. He had exactly one cousin, Adnan, whose grandmother had started coming to these reunions after she married Jace's great-uncle, and who had just come back from sitting shiva for a neighbor.

"Shiva," Adnan said, handing Jace a paper plate. "It's not the car. It's when people sit together for a week after somebody dies and everyone brings cake."

"Is it working?" Jace asked. "The cake part."

"The cake part thrives. The sad part, less so." Adnan shrugged. "People kept saying this phrase at the house. My mom said it about Mrs. Okonkwo. Olam ha-ba."

Jace wrote it down, spelled it wrong, fixed it. "What's it mean?"

"Okay, so, I asked my zayde, because I had to know too. He said it means 'the world to come.'" Adnan took a bite of someone's abandoned sandwich. "But here's the bizarre part. I asked him where it says that, like which page, because Hebrew school makes you look things up, and he laughed. He said the phrase itself isn't actually in the Hebrew Bible. Not once. People just call it that."

Jace stopped chewing. "Wait. It's the name for the Jewish afterlife, but it's not even in the book?"

"Olam ha-ba is the world to come, and no, the phrase isn't in the Hebrew Bible. That's what he said, and then he beat me at gin rummy."

This felt like a lead. Jace's dad was raised Catholic and still crossed himself near wasps, so Jace went looking for him by the horseshoe pit, where Uncle Roland was losing on purpose to make Grandpa feel like a champion.

"Dad. Catholics. After you die. Quick version."

His dad examined his horseshoe like it held the answer. "Heaven, hell, some waiting in between, depending on who you ask. God decides. Why is this urgent?"

"Science project," Jace said, which was not true, and everyone let it go because the potato salad was being unveiled.

He found a lawn chair and spread out his notes. Here was the puzzle. Nobody could show him either place. Heaven, olam ha-ba, all of it was like trying to find out what was inside a wrapped present without shaking it. But you could still learn something, he figured, by testing what people said. So he made a little chart. The variable he changed was who he asked. Uncle Roland, he knew, would say "heaven and that's that." Adnan's zayde had said the world to come, with the twist about the phrase. Grandpa would say something about fishing.

He tried his experiment at the dessert table, which guaranteed an audience.

"Grandpa, where do you go after you die?"

"Back in the ground, and if I'm lucky, somebody plants tomatoes over me." Grandpa pointed his fork at Jace. "Best fertilizer in the county."

"That's not an afterlife, that's compost."

"Compost is a kind of afterlife, kid. Ask the tomatoes."

Adnan appeared at his elbow, drawn by cake like a moth. "What did you write about me?"

Jace showed him the chart. Three columns, three answers, one big question mark at the bottom. "The problem is I can't check any of it. It's all invisible."

Adnan considered this while eating Jace's cake, which was a separate problem. "Zayde says that's the whole point. You do the good stuff now, in this world, and the other part takes care of itself." He licked his fork. "Also he says if you can't find it in the book, look harder, but he was laughing when he said it."

Jace wrote exactly that, word for word, and underlined the question mark twice. Then he looked at the empty spot where his cake had been.

"You ate my evidence."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: True lilies are highly toxic to cats, so they are unsafe to keep in a home with a cat.
story:
Arthur had planned this moment for six weeks, and the plan did not include a kitten asleep in a litter box. He stood in front of the small animal section at Pet Palace with his empty carrier in one hand and a list in the other, because Ms. Watanabe, his neighbour, had told him that list-makers made better pet owners than impulse buyers. He had come for a hamster. The list said so in his neatest printing.

Then a gray paw shot out between the bars of the cat enclosure and batted his pen onto the floor. The kitten that owned the paw looked at Arthur with an expression that said, yes, that was on purpose, what are you going to do about it. Aurelie, who had tagged along to supervise, leaned over his shoulder. "That one's provoking you," she said. "You have to respect the strategy." The cashier let Arthur hold the kitten, and after four minutes of purring directly into his ear, the hamster plan was dead.

"You'll need litter, food, a brush," the cashier said, ringing everything up. "And do yourself a favor. Before your cat comes home, walk around your house and look at your plants. Some of them are trouble." Arthur nodded the way people nod when they are mostly watching a kitten chew a cardboard corner.

At home, his mother's birthday was in full swing. His grandmother had arrived carrying an enormous bouquet, all tall stems and curling white flowers, and had set it proudly in the middle of the kitchen table. Arthur put the kitten's carrier down, and something about the flowers provoked a small alarm in the back of his brain. Plants are trouble. He crouched and studied the bouquet like a detective. The flowers had long stamens dusted with rusty powder, and thick stems, and they looked like the pictures from a book he had flipped through at school last spring, which had made him abruptly nervous then, too.

"Maina," he said into his phone, "you're the plant person. Those big white flowers, the ones with the pollen. What are they?" "True lilies," she said without hesitating. "Why?" "New kitten. Same house." There was a pause long enough to hear a page turn. "Oh no. Get those out of there. True lilies are really toxic to cats. You cannot have them in the house with a cat. At all." Arthur thanked her, hung up, and turned around to find the kitten already on the table, nose an inch from a petal.

He scooped the cat up with one hand, grabbed the vase with the other, and marched past his grandmother, his mother, and Ms. Watanabe, who raised her glass of sparkling cider in salute as he went. He set the bouquet on the porch rail, well away from the door, and came back inside. "Happy birthday, Mom," he said. "The flowers are beautiful. They're just not allowed in this house anymore." The kitten, watching from his arms, yawned hugely, as if to say the whole thing had been handled by professionals.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
story:
The rain was supposed to hit Fairview at six o'clock, and it was already quarter to. Sophie's mother had sent her to the gas station on Miller Road with ten dollars and one instruction: bring back D batteries, because the only flashlight in the house was dead and the power always went out on that street. Viola and Aayan had come along, and now all three of them stood in line behind six other people, all of them holding batteries, bottled water, or both.

The rack of D batteries had been full on Tuesday. Now it held four packs. Aayan pointed at the little sign taped to the shelf, which said the price had gone from five dollars to eight. "That's the owner being greedy," he said. "Sellers just pick whatever number they want."

"No, it's us," Viola said. "All these people grabbing batteries, that's why. Buyers decide, by what we'll pay." They went back and forth while the line shuffled forward, and the argument was starting to hinder Sophie's concentration, because she was counting packs and counting heads and the numbers did not look good.

Then she remembered something. Last summer she had pulled a fat old book off her uncle's shelf because she liked the cover, a green book called "Principles of Economics" by a man named Alfred Marshall, from 1890. She had only understood pieces of it, but one picture had stuck with her: a pair of scissors. Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors, and it takes both to set a price. Neither blade cuts alone. "You're both right," she said. "Aayan's right that Mr. Chowdhury sets the price, and Viola's right that we set it too, by fighting over four packs. Both blades. Scissors."

She tested it at the cooler on the way to the register. Bottled water, nearly gone, price up a dollar. Bags of chips, shelves still loaded, price stable, the same sticker as always. Plentiful, same price; scarce, higher price, with a whole line of buyers standing there proving which blade was doing the cutting. She grabbed a pack of D batteries and one bag of chips, and she still had enough from the ten.

When she got home, her mother was in the kitchen with the dead flashlight open on the counter. The wind had already started rattling the gutters. Sophie snapped in the batteries, clicked the switch, and the beam caught the ceiling just as the lights went out. "Two blades," she said, and set the flashlight on the table between them.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars; maggots grew in open jars, but not in jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat.
story:
Matthew wanted the corner of Ms. Addo's garden for a compost bin, and she had agreed, on one condition. "Show me it won't turn into a cloud of flies," she said, handing him two empty pasta jars. "Then you can invest your Saturdays in it."

Ashton did not believe flies could be stopped. "Rotting fruit makes flies," he said over the fence. "Everybody knows that. Leave a peach out and the flies just come out of it." Matthew said that was a guess, not a fact, and Ashton shrugged. "Fine, then prove it."

So Matthew made a test. He cut two equal chunks of overripe peach and dropped one into each jar. He left the first jar open on the garden wall, where flies could get in. Over the second jar he stretched a piece of gauze from the first-aid kit and screwed the ring down so the mesh sat flat and perpendicular to the jar's sides, covering the mouth completely. Nothing bigger than dust could pass through. He taped a note to the wall between them: open, covered, and the date.

"Flies come from the peach," Ashton said on the first day, tapping the covered jar. Matthew answered that the covered jar was the whole point. If flies appeared inside it, Ashton would be right. If they appeared only in the open jar, then something the gauze blocked had to be the real cause, even though Matthew could not watch every second to catch it happening.

Abdullah came by on the fourth afternoon and leaned over the jars without touching them. "The open one has maggots in it," he said. Matthew crouched down. Small white maggots wriggled on the peach chunk in the open jar, and two flies crawled along the inside of the glass. Abdullah checked the covered jar next, turning it in the light. The peach inside had gone brown and wet and sour-smelling, but no maggots, no flies, nothing moving. He held it up so Ashton could see through the gauze. "Same fruit, same heat, same days," Abdullah said. "Only difference is the lid."

That night Ms. Addo looked at both jars with a flashlight and then at Matthew's note. "Same result as a man in 1668," she said. "Francesco Redi. Meat in jars, and maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the ones covered with gauze that kept the flies off." Matthew wrote that down on his note, then added a line about his compost bin beside it. On Saturday morning he carried the bin to the corner of her garden and fitted the gauze frame over the top. Ashton watched from the fence and did not say anything. He just brought over a shovel.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
story:
Mathis stared at the blank poster board in the robotics club room and decided the problem was bigger than a broken sensor. The club was making a display for International Night, and Mr. Liu had taped a list of countries along the whiteboard, but half the club members said the names on the list were wrong. Not wrong exactly, but not theirs.

"Deutschland," said Kamila, pointing at the word Germany. "My cousin visited from there in the summer and laughed every time we called it Germany. She kept saying Deutschland until we said it back." She tapped the poster with her marker, defiant, like she dared anyone to argue.

Mr. Liu raised his eyebrows but said nothing, which was his way of telling them to figure it out themselves. Mathis wrote both words on a scrap of paper. He tested a simple idea: maybe every group had two names, one it used for itself and one outsiders used. He went around the room, asking each member what their families called themselves and what everyone else called them. Malory said her grandmother's town had an old name the map didn't use anymore. Another boy said his family's word for their people wasn't even close to the one in the textbook. The ratio of two names to one was holding up, every single time.

"There's a word for this," Kamila said, scrolling on the club's tablet. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym. A name outsiders use is an exonym. Like Deutschland and Germany."

"So we're all exonyming each other," Malory said, and the room laughed.

Mathis felt the problem sharpen. If they kept only the English names on the poster, the club members whose families used other words would walk past their own display and not see themselves in it. But he couldn't rewrite every label without asking people, and the night was only two meetings away. He proposed a fix: every label would show the endonym first, in larger letters, with the English name underneath in smaller ones. Some members worried the parents wouldn't recognize anything. Mr. Liu said the gym could accommodate a wider poster if they needed extra room.

They spent the rest of the meeting collecting names. Kamila wrote Deutschland in tall blue letters and stood back to check that it was straight. Mathis held the ruler while Malory penciled in her grandmother's town below the official one. At the end, Kamila stuck the marker behind her ear and said, "My cousin is going to see this photo and freak out."
